newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Higher interest income boosts NDB profits.
newsitem.headline: Higher interest income boosts NDB profits.

text.p: Sri Lanka's blue chip National Development Bank Ltd said on Monday that profits in the first six months to June had risen mainly due to growth in interest income and improved stock market conditions.
The development finance institution said net profits for six months to June rose 21 percent to 387.77 million from 321.14 million in the same period last year.
"Firstly, with the improved business climate several of the bank's clients in the hotel, textile and garment sectors were able to improve the servicing of their loans," the bank said in a statement.
"Secondly, the Colombo Stock Exchange performed strongly during the period and this enabled the bank to improve on its income from dividens and capital gains," it added.
Colombo's all share index had risen 39 percent this year to 841 points by Friday due to improved investor sentiment, brokers said.

The bank said business environment in the first half of 1997 had improved in contrast to 1996, mainly due to a better power supply and the government's ability to contain the northeast war, where Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels are fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils.
A severe drought in 1996, which led to average daily power cuts of five hours between March and August, badly affected industry and agriculture.
LTTE rebels bombed an oil depot, the Central Bank and a crowded commuter train in 1995 and 1996, hitting investor confidence.
Analysts said better-than-expected six-month results by NDB had led them to upgrade profit forecasts for the 12 months to December 1997.
"We had forecast a 13 percent growth to 760 million rupees from 670 million in 1996," said Nanda Nair, head of research at brokerage John Keells.
"After better-than-expected results in the first six months, our forecasts for the year could go to about 800 million," Nair added.

Channa Amaratunga, banking sector analyst at Asia Securities, said he too would be making an upward revision of forecasts. "We had forecast about a 10 percent growth in profits, but will now definitely have to make an upward revision".
But other analysts said they will rework numbers only after the bank has increased its issued capital by converting 27.5 million debentures now held by the Sri Lankan government.
The bank said last week that it will convert the debentures into 18.33 million ordinary shares in line with an early conversion agreement.
This would increase NDB's issued capital to 35.83 million shares from the current 17.5 million.
The bank's shares were trading at 290 rupees a 10-rupee share at 0625 GMT.
